title: Explaining encapsulation in an interview
question: An interviewer asks: "In your own words, what is encapsulation?" Which answer shows that you understand it?
options: Keeping an object's data private and letting it change only through methods that enforce its rules
Declaring every field private and generating a getter and a setter for each one automatically, which is all that the term really requires
Letting a subclass reuse the fields and methods of its parent without declaring them again
Hiding the class name behind an interface so that callers never learn which type they got
explanation: Encapsulation bundles state with the behaviour that works on it and exposes only a controlled interface, so the object can protect its invariants (for example, a balance never going negative). Generating a getter and a setter for every private field exposes the state again and enforces nothing. Reusing parent members is inheritance, and hiding the concrete type behind an interface is abstraction.

title: The four pillars with one real example
question: You are asked to explain the four pillars of OOP using a payment system. Which mapping is correct?
options: Encapsulation: the same `pay()` call behaves differently per type. Abstraction: `Account` guards its balance behind `withdraw`. Inheritance: callers use `PaymentMethod` without knowing the details. Polymorphism: `PixPayment` extends a base class

Encapsulation: `Account` guards its balance behind `withdraw`. Abstraction: callers use `PaymentMethod` without knowing the details. Inheritance: `PixPayment` and `CardPayment` extend a base class. Polymorphism: the same `pay()` call behaves differently per type

Encapsulation: `PixPayment` and `CardPayment` extend a base class. Abstraction: the same `pay()` call behaves differently per type. Inheritance: `Account` guards its balance. Polymorphism: callers use `PaymentMethod` without details

Encapsulation: callers use `PaymentMethod` without knowing the details. Abstraction: `PixPayment` and `CardPayment` extend a base class. Inheritance: the same `pay()` call behaves differently per type. Polymorphism: `Account` guards its balance
explanation: Encapsulation is protecting state behind methods, abstraction is exposing only what callers need, inheritance is a subtype extending a base type, and polymorphism is one call producing type-specific behaviour. The other mappings are plausible-sounding shuffles of those four ideas; a good answer also admits that inheritance is the pillar to use most carefully.

title: Overriding versus overloading
options: Both are overloads, because overriding is only possible when the parent method is declared abstract
`speak(int)` overrides because it adds behaviour to the parent, and `speak()` overloads because its signature is unchanged
`speak()` in `Dog` overrides the parent method (chosen at runtime by the real type), and `speak(int)` overloads it (chosen at compile time by the arguments)
Both are overrides, since both live in a subclass and share the name `speak` with the method in the parent class
explanation: Overriding replaces an inherited method with the same signature, and the version that runs depends on the object's runtime type. Overloading adds another method with the same name but different parameters, resolved at compile time from the argument types. A parent method does not need to be abstract to be overridden, and a different parameter list is exactly what makes a method an overload.

title: Abstract class or interface
question: An interviewer asks: "When would you pick an abstract class instead of an interface?" Which answer is accurate?
options: When you need multiple inheritance, because a class may extend several abstract classes but implement just one interface
When the type should never be instantiated, since an interface can always be instantiated through its default methods
When callers need faster dispatch, because abstract methods are resolved at compile time and interface methods at runtime, which matters in tight loops
When subclasses should share fields and common code; an interface only describes a contract that unrelated types can implement
explanation: An abstract class can carry instance state and constructor logic shared by closely related subclasses, but a class can extend only one of them. An interface is a contract that unrelated classes can implement, and a class can implement many. Both can be uncallable on their own (neither is instantiated directly), and both use runtime dispatch, so performance is not the criterion.

title: Why favour composition over inheritance
question: A hiring manager asks: "Why do many teams say to favour composition over inheritance?" Which answer is the most convincing?
options: A subclass depends on its parent's internals and inherits its whole API, while composition reuses behaviour through a field you can swap
Inheritance is slower at runtime because every inherited call walks up the class hierarchy before it finds the method to run, which adds up in large applications
Composition is required by every modern language, since newer compilers reject classes that extend another class
Inheritance cannot be combined with interfaces, so any class that implements one has to hold its collaborators by composition
explanation: Inheritance ties a subclass to its parent's implementation (changes upstream can break it) and exposes everything the parent exposes. Composition lets an object delegate to collaborators that can be replaced or tested separately. Method lookup cost is negligible, languages do not forbid inheritance, and classes can both extend a class and implement interfaces.

title: Equal objects missing from a HashSet
options: `equals` must be declared `static` for hash-based collections to be able to find it and call it
`hashCode` was not overridden, so equal points usually hash to different buckets and `equals` is never even called
`HashSet` compares elements with `==` and ignores `equals` entirely, so a second instance is never found, whatever the contents of its fields
The fields `x` and `y` are not `final`, and `HashSet` refuses to look up objects that have mutable fields
explanation: The contract says that equal objects must return the same hash code. A hash-based collection first uses `hashCode` to pick a bucket, and only then calls `equals` among the entries there; the default identity hash code puts two separate instances in different buckets. `equals` is an instance method, `HashSet` does use it, and mutable fields are allowed (though mutating them after insertion is risky).

title: A class with only final fields that is not immutable
options: Immutable classes must also mark each field `volatile`, otherwise other threads may keep seeing a stale list
`final` is enforced only at compile time, so any class can be changed by reflection and none can ever be immutable
`final` only stops the reference from being reassigned; callers can still change the list they passed in or the one `getItems` returns
The class needs setters that validate their input, because without them callers have no safe way to change an order
explanation: `final` fixes the reference, not the object it points to. Because the constructor keeps the caller's list and the getter hands it out, anyone holding it can add or remove items. The fix is a defensive copy in and a read-only view or copy out (for example `List.copyOf`). `volatile` is about visibility, reflection tricks are not the design concern, and setters would make the class mutable, not immutable.

title: A long chain of getters in a condition
options: Make `customer`, `address` and `country` public fields, which removes the three getter calls and shortens the line
Store the country in a static global so that any class can read it without going through `Order` at all
Wrap the whole chain in a `try/catch` for `NullPointerException` so that a missing address no longer crashes
Add something like `order.isDomestic()`, so the caller tells `Order` what it needs and `Address` can change without breaking callers
explanation: A chain of getters couples the caller to the structure of three classes, so any change to `Address` ripples outward (the "train wreck" smell, related to the Law of Demeter). Moving the question into `Order` keeps that knowledge in one place and follows "tell, don't ask". Public fields couple even more, globals hide dependencies, and catching `NullPointerException` hides the design problem.

title: What idempotent means for PUT and DELETE
question: An interviewer says "PUT and DELETE are idempotent, but POST is not". What does idempotent mean here?
options: The server returns exactly the same status code and body every time the request is repeated
The request is only a read, so repeating it can never change anything stored on the server
Repeating the identical request leaves the server in the same state as sending it once
The response can be cached by browsers and proxies, so a repeat never reaches the origin
explanation: An idempotent method has the same intended effect on the server whether it runs once or many times: deleting user 5 twice still leaves user 5 deleted, even though the second response may be 404 instead of 204. That is different from "safe" (read-only, like GET), from identical responses, and from cacheability. It is why clients may retry PUT and DELETE after a timeout but must be careful with POST.

title: Choosing between 401 and 403
question: A signed-in member with a valid token calls `DELETE /admin/users/5`. Only admins may do this. Which status code fits best?
options: 401 Unauthorized, because every refusal connected to permissions should use it
405 Method Not Allowed, because this caller is not permitted to use DELETE
400 Bad Request, because the request breaks a business rule of the application
403 Forbidden, because the caller is identified but not allowed to do this
explanation: 401 means the request lacks valid authentication (missing, expired or invalid credentials), so the client should authenticate and try again. 403 means the server understood who the caller is and refuses anyway, which is this case. 405 describes a resource that does not support the method for anyone, and 400 is for malformed requests.

title: What happens when you type a URL
question: You type `https://shop.example/cart` and press Enter. An interviewer asks for the main steps, in order. Which sequence is right?
options: Resolve the hostname with DNS, open a TCP connection and finish the TLS handshake, send the HTTP request, then parse the HTML and fetch the CSS, JS and images it references
Open the TLS connection first, send the HTTP request, and only afterwards resolve the hostname with DNS using an address the server returns in its reply
Download the CSS, JS and images first, then resolve the hostname with DNS and finally ask the server for the HTML page that references them
Resolve the hostname with DNS, send the HTTP request in plain text, and upgrade to TLS only if the server answers with an error status code
explanation: The browser needs an IP address before it can connect, so DNS comes first. Then it opens a TCP connection and, for HTTPS, completes the TLS handshake before any HTTP data is sent. The server answers with HTML, and the browser parses it and requests the subresources it discovers. Resources cannot be fetched before the HTML names them, and HTTPS never starts in plain text and upgrades after an error.

title: Session cookie versus bearer token
question: A candidate is asked how a session cookie differs from a bearer token kept in JavaScript memory and sent in the `Authorization` header. Which answer is accurate at a basic level?
options: A cookie is always encrypted by the browser, while a bearer token travels in clear text even when the site uses HTTPS
The browser sends a cookie automatically (hence the CSRF defenses); a header token is sent only when your code adds it
A cookie can hold only a numeric user id, but a bearer token can carry any claims, so only tokens can identify a user
Cookies work only on pages served over plain HTTP, so any site that uses HTTPS must authenticate with bearer tokens instead
explanation: Cookies are stored and sent by the browser automatically for matching requests, which is convenient but is exactly why CSRF defenses (such as `SameSite`) matter; `HttpOnly` also keeps scripts from reading them. A token in a header must be attached by your code, so it is not sent automatically, but anything JavaScript can read can be stolen by XSS. Neither claim about encryption, size or HTTP-only cookies is true.

title: Explaining a CORS error in one sentence
question: A front end on `http://localhost:3000` calls an API on `http://localhost:5000`. The browser console shows a CORS error, yet the same request works with curl. What is the right explanation and fix?
options: The API rejected the call as unauthorized, so the front end must add `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` to its own request headers
The operating system firewall blocks browsers from reaching port 5000 but not curl, so the port must be opened to browser traffic
The browser blocks the response unless the API sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` for that origin; fix it in the API
Curl and browsers negotiate different HTTP versions, so the API has to downgrade to HTTP/1.0 whenever a browser is the client
explanation: CORS is enforced by the browser: the request reaches the API, but the script may read the response only if the API opts in with CORS headers such as `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. Curl is not a browser and ignores the policy. Adding the header to the request is meaningless because it is a response header, and neither firewalls nor HTTP versions are involved.

title: Finding customers who never ordered
question: Tables: `customers(id, name)` and `orders(id, customer_id)`. You must list customers that have never placed an order. Which query does that?
options: SELECT c.name FROM customers c INNER JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL
SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id = NULL
SELECT c.name FROM customers c RIGHT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE c.id IS NULL
SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL
explanation: A LEFT JOIN keeps every customer and fills the order columns with NULL when nothing matches, so filtering on `o.id IS NULL` leaves exactly the customers without orders. An INNER JOIN drops unmatched customers, so nothing is left to filter. `= NULL` is never true (it needs `IS NULL`), and the RIGHT JOIN version starts from orders and returns no customer names.

title: Slow bulk import on an over-indexed table
question: A reporting table has 12 indexes added over time "just in case". A nightly import of 20 million rows now takes hours, although queries on the table are fast. What best explains the slow import, and what is a sensible response?
options: Each inserted row must also be written into all 12 indexes, so drop the unused ones or drop and rebuild them around the bulk load
Indexes lock the whole table for every insert, so lowering the transaction isolation level removes the lock and the slowdown
The indexes became stale after the last import, so running `REINDEX` on all of them before each import restores insert speed
Insert speed depends only on the row width, so the right fix is to move the long text columns into a separate table, which keeps each row small
explanation: Indexes speed up reads at the price of writes: every insert (and most updates and deletes) must maintain each index, so 12 of them multiply the work. Keep only the indexes that real queries use, and for a large load consider dropping and recreating indexes afterwards. Indexes do not lock the whole table per insert, they are not made "stale" by an import, and row width is only one factor among several.

title: Fixing an N+1 query pattern
question:
orders = repo.findLatest(100)
for o in orders:
  print(o.customer.name)  // lazy load: SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id = ?
The endpoint runs 101 queries and is slow. A teammate proposes adding an index on `orders.customer_id`. What should you say?
options: That index will make each lookup instant and bring the total down to a single query for the whole page
The number of queries must stop depending on the order count: use a join, eager load or one `IN (...)` query
Raising the page size to 1000 will fetch more rows per round trip and cut the number of queries sent to the database
Running the 100 customer lookups in parallel threads turns the 101 queries into one, because the database merges them
explanation: The cost here is 1 + N round trips: one query for the orders and one per order for its customer. An index only makes each of those queries cheaper, it does not reduce their number (and customers are already looked up by primary key). Fix the pattern by loading the related rows together, with a join or eager loading, or in one batched `WHERE id IN (...)` query. Parallelism and bigger pages do not merge queries.

title: First move in a live coding interview
question: The interviewer reads a problem aloud and shares a blank editor. What is the best first move?
options: Restate the problem in your own words, ask about inputs and limits, and confirm your understanding with a small example
Start typing the optimal solution right away, since showing speed early signals confidence and skill to the interviewer
Stay quiet while you read the statement again for a few minutes so that your first words will be perfectly formed
Ask the interviewer which algorithm they consider the best fit, so you will not waste time on the wrong approach
explanation: Restating and clarifying shows that you listen, catches misunderstandings before they cost you twenty minutes, and gives the interviewer a first look at how you think. Rushing into code risks solving the wrong problem, long silence hides your reasoning, and asking for the algorithm hands over the part they are trying to evaluate.

title: Clarifying questions for a duplicates problem
question: The task: "Write a function that finds the duplicates in a list of integers." Which set of clarifying questions would an interviewer value most?
options: Which language the company uses in production, and whether the solution has to follow that team's style guide
How large the list can be, whether it may be empty or unsorted, and whether to return the first duplicate or every one
Whether sorting is the intended approach, and whether you may call a library function that already removes duplicates, since that choice may affect the rest of your plan
Whether the code will be reviewed afterwards, and whether the interviewer wants comments on every line of the answer
explanation: Good questions pin down the specification: input size and shape (empty, unsorted, negative values), and the expected output (first duplicate, all of them, each once or with counts). They also steer the choice between a sort, a set or a counter. Asking about house style, hinting at the answer you want, or about review and comments does not reduce the ambiguity in the problem.

title: When only the slow solution comes to mind
question: In a "find two numbers that add up to a target" problem, the only idea you have is two nested loops, O(n²). Ten minutes remain. What do interviewers reward most?
options: Keep thinking in silence until the optimal solution appears, since presenting a slow version would count against you
Write the nested loops quickly without comment and hope the interviewer will not ask about the running time
Say that it is a brute-force O(n²) solution, get it working, then discuss how a lookup structure could speed it up
Tell the interviewer that the problem is unfair for a junior position and ask to be given an easier one instead
explanation: A correct brute force is a solid baseline: say what it is and what it costs, make it work, and then reason aloud about the bottleneck (the repeated search for the complement, which a hash-based lookup can make O(1)). This shows structured thinking and progress under time pressure. Silence and hidden complexity give the interviewer nothing to evaluate, and complaining about difficulty reflects badly.

title: Answering "what is the complexity?"
question: You finished a solution with a loop inside a loop where the inner one can stop early. The interviewer asks for its complexity and you are unsure. What is the best way to answer?
options: Answer O(n) because you can see only one `for` keyword that scans the input, then change the subject
Say that complexity does not matter for small inputs and that you would measure it with a benchmark later, once the code runs in production
Wait for the interviewer to give the answer, since guessing wrong is worse than admitting you do not know
Reason aloud about the worst case in terms of input size, state time and space, and say where you could improve it
explanation: Interviewers care about the reasoning more than a memorised label. Walk through the loops, name n, consider the worst case (when the early exit never triggers), state time and space, and mention an improvement you would try. Guessing from keywords is often wrong, dismissing the question looks careless, and going silent ends the conversation you are supposed to have.

title: What to do once the code is written
question: You just finished typing a solution in a live coding interview and there are 8 minutes left. Which behaviour do interviewers reward most?
options: Say that it is done because it compiles, then wait for the interviewer to run their own tests against it
Run only the example from the problem statement, and stop as soon as it prints the expected output, then say that the solution is complete
Rewrite the whole solution in a more compact style, since fewer lines usually mean fewer possible bugs
Trace the example by hand, then try edge cases such as empty, single element and duplicates, and fix what you find aloud
explanation: Checking your own work is a core job skill. Tracing a sample input shows you understand what the code does, and edge cases (empty input, one element, duplicates, negatives, large values) are where bugs hide. Finding and fixing a bug aloud counts in your favour. Compiling is not correctness, one happy-path example proves little, and a late rewrite adds risk without verification.

title: Naming and readability under time pressure
question: With 15 minutes left, your working code uses names such as `a`, `b`, `tmp` and one 40-line function. What is the best way to handle readability?
options: Leave it, because interviewers only check whether the output is correct and never read the code itself
Add a long comment above every line to explain what each cryptic name stands for in the algorithm, so the intent is documented
Rename to descriptive names, extract a small helper if it is quick, and say what else you would clean up with more time
Replace the loop with the shortest clever one-liner you can think of, even if it takes a minute to decode
explanation: Interviewers read the code as a preview of what a pull request from you would look like. Clear names and one small helper cost seconds, and naming the cleanup you would do next shows judgment about trade-offs. Comments cannot replace good names, clever one-liners hurt readability, and the idea that only output counts ignores what the exercise is meant to reveal.

title: Being stuck and receiving a hint
question: You have been stuck for 8 minutes and have said little. The interviewer offers a hint: "What if you could check whether you have already seen a value in constant time?" Which response is strongest?
options: Keep going with your original approach to show independence, and ignore the hint unless you are completely out of ideas
Thank them, say what you now understand, connect the hint to your current attempt, and continue narrating the new plan
Say that this is exactly what you were about to do, then implement it in silence so that it looks like it was your idea
Ask the interviewer to write the key line of code, so that you can spend the remaining time on the easier parts
explanation: Hints are part of the interview, and what is evaluated is how you receive them: listen, show how the hint changes your model (a lookup structure for seen values), and keep reasoning aloud. Claiming the idea was yours is dishonest and usually obvious, ignoring help signals poor collaboration, and handing over the hardest line gives away the part being assessed. Also, saying earlier that you are stuck and what you have tried would have helped.

title: Submitting a take-home assignment
question: A take-home asks for a small REST API for a to-do list, suggesting about 4 hours. The core works and you have time left. Which submission is most likely to impress a reviewer?
options: Met requirements, tests for key behaviour, small clear commits and a README covering how to run it, decisions made and what you would do next
The same core plus authentication, caching, a message queue and a microservice split, to prove that you can handle larger systems
The core with no README or tests, because clean code should be self-explanatory and extra files only distract the reviewer
A polished front end with animations and theming added on top, since appearance is the first thing that a reviewer sees
explanation: Reviewers want to see that you read the requirements, deliver a working core, test the behaviour that matters, and explain your decisions. A README (how to run, assumptions, trade-offs, next steps) and tidy commits make the work easy to evaluate. Adding unrequested features is scope creep (YAGNI) and creates more code to review, skipping tests and docs looks careless, and unrequested UI polish does not address the brief.
